segs.text: Patched, not rebuilt. How a ligament heals after a sprain, and why it is different from muscle.
Muscle and ligament go through the same repair steps.
But only one of them can actually rebuild itself.
The other patches the hole with scar, and it never fully goes back to the original.
A ligament is mostly type I collagen, arranged in tight parallel bundles.
It has very few cells and a poor blood supply.
Most of its vessels, nerves, and backup cells live in the outer layer, the epiligament.
Ligaments also contain mechanoreceptors that tell the brain where the joint is.
Clinical tie-in. Compared with muscle.
Muscle is packed with blood vessels and has satellite cells under every fiber.
Ligament has neither, so it has to recruit help from outside.
Stecco link: the epiligament plays the same role for ligament that the epimysium and deep fascia play for muscle. It is the gliding, vessel-rich, cell-supplying envelope.
When the fibers snap, the ligament cells lose the tension they depend on, and many of them die within hours.
Bleeding comes mostly from the torn epiligament.
Unlike muscle, there's no contraction band to seal anything.
That is a muscle-fiber feature only.
Grade I: stretched fibers.
Grade II: a partial tear.
Grade III: a complete tear, with joint laxity.
The first five days look almost exactly like muscle:
clot, growth factors, and a flood of neutrophils.
The fibrin clot becomes the temporary scaffold that everything else will build on.
Clinical tie-in. Protect the scaffold.
Protect, compress, elevate.
For a Grade III ankle sprain, a short period of rigid support, 10 days or less, is reasonable.
Avoid long casting.
Macrophages, T cells, VEGF, and new blood vessels peak between days 5 and 9,
a few days later than in muscle.
Most of this activity starts in the epiligament,
and then moves into the gap as granulation tissue.
Clinical tie-in. Same handoff, later.
Same M1 → M2 handoff as in muscle.
The same NSAID caution applies (see Scene 9).
Ligament-specific human data are limited.
Type III collagen gene activity peaks around day 7,
and continues for at least four weeks, mostly in the new scar.
Type I collagen starts early too, peaking around days 7 to 14,
both in the scar and at the old ends.
From about day 9, cell death takes over as the overcrowded site thins itself out.
In muscle, new fibers push down basement-membrane tunnels.
In ligament, only collagen threads fill the gap.
Clinical tie-in. The weakest window.
This is the weakest window.
Functional treatment, meaning early weight bearing with a brace or tape plus balance and neuromuscular exercise, beats immobilization for return to sport, swelling, and satisfaction in ankle sprains.
Loading tells the fibroblasts which direction to lay collagen.
For months, fibroblasts keep making collagen
and slowly line it up along the lines of load.
Myofibroblasts pull the scar together.
But athletes often return to play long before this scar has matured.
Ankle sprain return to sport is typically about one week for Grade I, two weeks for Grade II, and four weeks for Grade III.
The scar is still maturing the whole time. That mismatch is why the next phase of rehab matters.
Cross-linking and alignment continue for 6 to 12 months,
and some remodeling goes on for years.
The final tissue is scar: ligament-like, but with more type III collagen, thinner and less organized fibrils, and lower strength.
In closely related tendon research, repaired tissue reaches up to 30% lower tensile strength.
The scar may also heal slightly long, and the joint's position sensors are disrupted.
Clinical tie-in. Why sprains come back.
This explains recurrent sprains and chronic ankle instability.
Balance and proprioceptive training reduces re-injury over 7–12 months.
The MCL heals well on its own.
The ACL almost never does.
It floats in synovial fluid, so a stable clot can't form between the ends.
The unstable knee also keeps shifting, which works against healing.
ACL cells and the ACL's epiligament also behave differently from the MCL's.
Bridge-enhanced ACL repair places a scaffold soaked in the patient's own blood into the gap, giving the clot something to hold onto.
Clinical tie-in. ACL: what this means.
Reconstruction remains standard.
Bridge-enhanced ACL repair (BEAR) places a scaffold soaked in the patient's own blood into the gap to give the clot something to hold onto.
It was non-inferior to autograft reconstruction at 2 years in a randomized trial, although re-tear risk may be higher.
Here is where each treatment acts on the healing timeline.
Brief protection, days 0 to 10 for Grade III: protect the clot so the scaffold can form.
Early protected loading: load is the signal that lines up the collagen.
Balance and proprioception training: retrain the joint's GPS.
NSAIDs: short use for pain is common; long courses may blunt repair signaling. Ligament-specific human data are limited.
Acetaminophen: pain relief with less effect on local repair signals.
Shockwave and PRP: growth-factor and vessel signaling, with animal and limited human data.
Manual therapy and movement around the epiligament and fascia may help gliding and stiffness in the subacute and remodeling phases. Lasting structural effects are unproven.
Same blueprint, different builders.
Muscle rebuilds itself and leaves a thin seam.
Ligament fills the gap with a patch that hardens for a year.
Side by side: how each tissue heals, who rebuilds it, and what rehab has to focus on.
Rehab has to respect that timeline: the athlete feels ready long before the tissue is.
Muscle regrows. Ligament patches. Feeling better isn't the same as being healed.
